title: Temporal gating warmup fieldnotes
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad for experiments exploring "temporal gating" during warmup. Observed recurring p99 spikes after rolling restarts; hypothesis is that scheduler gating during early warmup + small burst arrivals amplifies tail. This doc contains test plan, run notes, raw sample numbers, quick plots (ASCII), and immediate next actions.

Background / hypothesis:
- We bias warmup to gradually open concurrency via a gating window (e.g., allow 2->4->8 concurrent requests across the first N seconds) to avoid cache thrash and OOM spikes.
- If the gating steps align with incoming microbursts, the effective instantaneous concurrency jumps cause transient scheduling contention (kernel wakes, allocator churn) that inflates p95/p99.
- Goal: characterize whether gating timing or step-size is dominant, and whether adding small randomized jitter in gate-open time reduces the tail.

Test environment:
- Model: open-weights-13b (kv-cache warmup sensitive)
- Runtime build: serving-runtime v0.52.1 (profiling-enabled)
- Hardware: single A100-80GB (shared ci bench node), CUDA 12.1
- Container: rwinference/bench:2026-02-15
- Traffic generator: go-bench-proxy v0.9 (Poisson and custom-arrival modes)
- Metric collection: Prometheus scrape @5s, traces via jaeger lite

Warmup gating configs tested:
A) linear-small: gate steps [2,4,8] at T = [0s, 6s, 18s]
B) linear-big: gate steps [4,8,16] at T = [0s, 8s, 24s]
C) jittered: linear-small + uniform jitter +/-20% applied to each step time
D) instant-open: no gating (control)

Workload patterns:
- baseline-poisson: Poisson arrivals, mean QPS 20, T=5s warmup window (steady-ish)
- microburst-train: repeated tiny bursts: 200ms bursts at 80rps for 3s every 30s (to simulate frontend batching)
- long-tail-staccato: random spikes 0.5–2s long at up to 150% of baseline

Procedure (per run):
1) cold start process, ensure no prior kv cache (restart runtime)
2) apply gating config and start traffic generator
3) run for 10 minutes, collect percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99/p999), request counts, and OOM/eviction logs
4) snapshot kernel wake traces for first 30s of every minute (if p95>threshold)

Representative results (excerpt):
- Run: microburst-train under linear-small
  - p50 = 32ms, p90 = 72ms, p95 = 110ms, p99 = 420ms, p999 = 980ms
  - Observed ~3 spikes >1s coincident with gate steps (6s and 18s) and arrival bursts aligning within +/-200ms window.

- Run: microburst-train under jittered
  - p50 = 34ms, p90 = 75ms, p95 = 115ms, p99 = 180ms, p999 = 340ms
  - Spikes reduced by ~57% at p99 compared to linear-small. No >1s outliers recorded.

- Run: microburst-train under instant-open (control)
  - p50 = 30ms, p90 = 70ms, p95 = 105ms, p99 = 160ms, p999 = 310ms
  - Baseline tail similar to jittered for this workload; suggests gating introduced extra coupling with arrival pattern.

Notes from traces / profiler:
- Kernel wake patterns: at gate-open times we saw dense wakeup events from allocator threads and CV notify flood; context-switch spikes aligned to the p99 windows.
- Memory allocator: short-lived bump in device-side allocator calls (dev-malloc) around gating steps. Eviction logs show small KV cache churn at step boundaries.
- GC pause: python-side GC noise small; not primary driver.

Quick ascii latency timeline (microburst-train, linear-small):
Time(s) | 0      5      10     15     20     25
p99(ms) | 40 ---- 120 --- 420 --- 90 ---- 480 --- 70
             ^gate@6s    ^gate@18s     ^burst every 30s

Interpretation / tentative conclusions:
- Temporal gating can interact badly with periodic microbursts. If a burst coincides with a gate-open event, resources (allocators, kernel threads, IO scheduling) spike causing long tails.
- Randomizing gate timings (jittered) mostly mitigates the worst tails while keeping warmup behavior similar.
- For realistic production traffic which is not perfectly Poisson, the cost of gating (in tail risk) may outweigh the benefits unless we incorporate randomness or per-instance phase offsets.

Immediate action items:
- Short-term (next week): add <50% jitter to gating config in canary cluster; instrument kernel wake counts and eviction rates per gate event. Link PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/242 (draft).
- Mid-term: prototype per-instance phase offset seeding (hash of instance id) to avoid fleet-wide synchronized gates. Run A/B vs jitter.
- Long-term: investigate allocator backpressure mechanisms (batched dev-alloc/freelist thawing) to avoid mass alloc wakes at gate times.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How sensitive is this to model size/kv footprint? Need a run on 70B distill (if we can access heavy nodes).
- Does changing gate step cardinality (smaller increments e.g., 2->3->4) meaningfully lower p99 vs adding jitter? Quick experiment idea: micro-steps + jitter.
- Might also test spreading warmup over longer wall time (flatten) vs gating steps — tradeoff vs cold latency exposure.

Logs attached (short excerpts pasted):
- eviction_log snippet: "2026-02-20T12:06:05Z eviction: kv: 12 entries removed, peak_latency=587ms"
- trace snippet: "kernel_wakeup: 118 events at t=6005..6030ms coincident with batch_dispatch spike"

Personal notes:
- This is a messy scratchpad. If results look promising, I'll formalize into a bench brief and a small PR to add jitter support to our gating config. For now, tag as exploratory and keep the canary conservative.

Next run plan (short):
- Run micro-steps (2->3->4->6) with 30% jitter, microburst-train, 4 repeats; capture p99 and kernel_wakeup counts. Compare against instant-open control.
- Owner for next run: @Marta Lee (I'll share bench node creds).

End of notes.
